transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this to 45 minutes. quick roll call?
[00:06] Ravi: Ravi here, ML lead. Sofia and Lydia are on.
[00:10] Sofia: Yep, good afternoon.
[00:12] Jordan: Jordan from Redwood, SE on the call.
[00:15] Maya: Cool. Agenda: brief benchmark review, TTFT issues we saw on streaming, kernel choices for longer sequences, and next steps.
[00:25] Ravi: Thanks. So from our side we ran the 8k sequence test overnight against the dedicate-like config you shared. We saw p50 latency ok, but TTFT for first token is spiking around 320ms which is... higher than we expected.
[00:38] Jordan: Yeah we saw that in the logs too. I pulled the traces — looks like the streaming path is initiating a new CUDA context and doing a small JIT step before the first token is emitted, adding ~180-220ms. There's also a kernel select step for fused attention that can add overhead if the sequence length falls outside the expected bucket.
[00:55] Sofia: Is that specific to your hosted runtime or would we see the same on our infra?
[00:59] Jordan: It's a mix. Some of the overhead is in the runtime orchestration—initializing streaming session and KV cache allocation. On your infra, depending on kernel libs and cuDNN/cuda driver versions, you might see similar or slightly different magnitudes. We did notice Anthropic and some in-house infra people use a "warm-up" jitter to avoid the worst TTFT, but that increases cost.
[01:22] Ravi: Warm-up jitter isn't ideal for us. We care about first-interaction latency for real-time use cases.
[01:26] Maya: Understood. Jordan, can you walk through the two main contributors we identified?
[01:30] Jordan: Sure. One: session start/stream handshake and KV cache prefill. Two: kernel selection + small JIT / memory plan when sequence length hits 4k-8k ranges. For the first one we can optimize by keeping streaming sessions warm for pinned users or use a fast path that skips KV prefill when context length is small. For the second, we recommend pre-selecting the kernel based on your expected token distribution—if you expect lots of long sequences, pick the long-seq kernels and accept slightly higher per-token cost for smaller sequences.
[01:56] Lydia: How much do the kernel choices affect throughput vs TTFT?
[01:59] Jordan: Quantitatively, in our test cluster: pre-selecting long-seq kernel reduces TTFT by ~120ms on average for 8k sequences because it avoids the JIT step. However, per-token throughput at short seqs can drop 5-12% depending on microkernel. Also quantization settings matter—4-bit QAT-ish paths had different kernel codepaths that sometimes increased compile time.
[02:25] Ravi: We're also seeing some variance in streaming chunk sizes — sometimes the client sends a 64-token chunk, sometimes 256. Does chunk size interact here?
[02:33] Jordan: Yes, chunk size affects how quickly the runtime can emit first token after planning. Smaller initial chunks can trigger the streaming emit faster but may also prevent efficient batching for subsequent tokens. There's a trade-off: small chunk -> faster TTFT but potentially higher per-token compute overhead downstream.
[02:50] Sofia: What about prefix/KV caching—can we precompute prefixes to reduce runtime work?
[02:54] Jordan: If you have common prefixes (e.g., system prompts), yes precomputing KV cache and storing them removes a chunk of work at session start. In practice we saw TTFT drop ~80-100ms when using prefix caching for a 2k prompt. For 8k sequences, the savings scale but so does memory footprint.
[03:12] Maya: We prepared an updated benchmark sheet — Maya: link to sheet in meeting chat: https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/atlas-2026-03-10. It has TTFT, p50, p90 for streaming and batch modes.
[03:22] Ravi: Quick note — the p90 numbers look better for batch, but streaming p90 is painful.
[03:27] Jordan: Right. Batch hides the per-request orchestration cost by filling bigger microbatches; streaming needs a different approach.
[03:33] Sophie: Sorry, Sofia.
[03:34] Sofia: No worries.
[03:36] Jordan: Proposed experiment set: A) Streaming-first config: keep streaming session warm for pinned user tokens and preselect long-seq kernels when incoming token distribution shows >30% >2k. B) Batch-hybrid: accumulate up to 128 tokens or 100ms window before first emit to allow batching benefits. C) Prefix-cache heavy: precompute top-10 prefixes. We expect A to give best TTFT for long sessions, B to give better avg throughput, C to help predictable prompts.
[04:04] Ravi: How safe is A for cost — warmed sessions mean extra reserved resources?
[04:09] Jordan: It depends on policy — we can keep lightweight warm handles that don't reserve full GPU memory but reduce orchestration. Alternatively, Dedicated capacity reservations could be used (cost higher but stable latency). We can estimate cost delta — Jordan: we'll add that to the sheet.
[04:24] Maya: Quick qualifier: customer wants <200ms TTFT for first interaction 90% of the time. Is that realistic on 8k sequences?
[04:32] Jordan: Tough but possible with prefix caching + preselected kernels + warmed sessions. With the streaming-first config we saw TTFT ~170-190ms p90 on our 8k sim in the lab after optimizations. However real-world variance and driver differences might push it up.
[04:48] Ravi: Great. For kernel profiling, what traces do you need from our side?
[04:52] Jordan: We need the anonymized perf traces showing the JIT/compile phases, the timestamps for CUDA kernel launches, and the client chunk timings. A simple script we provide can collect those and redact PII. I'll drop the profiler checklist in the chat and upload to the benchmark sheet.
[05:08] Maya: Action items recap: Jordan will upload kernel profiling checklist and run a baseline on Redwood cluster; Ravi will share sample 8k workload; Maya will post updated benchmark TL;DR in CRM.
[05:18] Sofia: Can we also get an estimate of cost delta between streaming-first and batch-hybrid?
[05:22] Jordan: Yes, we'll add cost estimates per 1M tokens and per-concurrent-user for both configs.
[05:28] Lydia: Any security or compliance blockers if we use warmed sessions or prefix caching?
[05:32] Maya: No new blockers; warmed sessions are an operational mode. For prefix caching we'd respect customer data policies — if prefix contains PHI we recommend not caching or using encrypted KMS-backed caches. We can tie cache TTL to retention policy.
[05:49] Ravi: Makes sense.
[05:51] Jordan: Ok last thing — we noticed a small transcription artifact in logs where model name shows as "Redwood-llm-3" but your config uses an open LLaMA derivative; just mismatch in naming, not functional.
[06:03] Maya: Good catch. Any other questions?
[06:06] Sofia: No, thanks.
[06:08] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll reconvene after the profiling runs — suggest next Wednesday unless earlier results prompt us.
[06:15] Ravi: Works for us.
[06:17] Maya: End.
